items.stem: Which of the following best defines 'pure economic loss'?
options: Financial loss that is not consequential on physical damage to the claimant or their property, which is generally not recoverable in negligence.
Where the defendant's breach made a material (more than minimal) contribution to the damage, it may be treated as a cause (Bonnington Castings v Wardlaw).
A relationship in which the defendant has special skill, knows the claimant will rely on the advice for a particular purpose, and the reliance is reasonable (Hedley Byrne; Caparo).
A new intervening act of a third party, the claimant or a natural event that breaks the chain of causation between breach and damage.
items.answer: Financial loss that is not consequential on physical damage to the claimant or their property, which is generally not recoverable in negligence.
items.markingKey: pure economic loss: Financial loss that is not consequential on physical damage to the claimant or their property, which is generally not recoverable in negligence.

The test for whether a tort was committed in the course of employment: whether it was so closely connected with the employment that it is fair and just to hold the employer liable (Lister v Hesley Hall).
A partial defence under the Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945 where the claimant's own fault contributed to the damage, so damages are reduced by a just and equitable amount.

items.stem: Explain how the courts deal with acceptance by email.
items.answer: Email is treated like an instantaneous method (Entores, Brinkibon), so acceptance is generally effective when received; during office hours it is received when it arrives (Thomas v BPE); the Electronic Commerce Regulations 2002 deal with online orders.

items.stem: On 1 March Ines agreed to work as a sound engineer for Daniel's travel company from 1 June. On 10 April Daniel told Ines, "We will not need you after all." Advise Ines on the options available. Consider all the relevant issues and reach a justified conclusion.
items.answer: Law: anticipatory breach: a party indicates before performance is due that it will not perform (Hochster v De la Tour); the innocent party may accept the repudiation and sue at once, or affirm and wait; waiting risks the contract being frustrated (Avery v Bowden); performance after affirming requires a legitimate interest (White and Carter v McGregor); Ines must mitigate loss by seeking other work. Application: Daniel's statement on 10 April is an anticipatory breach; Ines can sue immediately without waiting for 1 June; Ines should look for other work to mitigate. Conclusion: Ines can accept the repudiation and claim damages immediately, subject to the duty to mitigate.

items.stem: Arjun went to hospital in Nairobi with severe stomach pains. The doctor negligently failed to examine Arjun and sent Arjun home. Arjun later suffered permanent damage that prompt treatment would have prevented. Advise whether the hospital is liable. Your answer should explain the relevant law, refer to decided cases and reach a reasoned conclusion.
items.answer: Law: factual causation: but for the breach, would the harm have occurred? (Barnett v Chelsea and Kensington HMC); the hospital owes a duty and breached it by failing to examine, but breach alone is not enough. Application: Arjun later suffered permanent damage that prompt treatment would have prevented; this satisfies the but for test, so the hospital is liable. Conclusion: This satisfies the but for test, so the hospital is liable.

items.stem: Arjun works for Leila Ltd as a delivery driver in Lisbon. Against orders, Arjun gave a lift to Grace, a hitchhiker, who was injured when Arjun crashed. Advise Grace whether Leila Ltd is vicariously liable.
items.answer: Law: stage 1: employee or relationship akin to employment (Ready Mixed Concrete; Catholic Child Welfare Society; Barclays 2020); stage 2: tort closely connected with employment (Lister v Hesley Hall; Mohamud v Morrison); prohibited acts in the course of the job (Limpus; Rose v Plenty) v acts outside it (Twine; Hilton - frolic). Application: Arjun is an employee of Leila Ltd; the tort was not for the employer's business, so probably outside the course of employment (Twine v Bean's Express). Conclusion: Leila Ltd is liable only if the tort was in the course of employment: here it was not for the employer's business, so probably outside the course of employment (Twine v Bean's Express).

items.stem: Evaluate the doctrine of privity of contract. Your answer should consider arguments on both sides and reach a conclusion.
items.answer: For: protects parties' freedom of contract; prevents people being bound by contracts they did not agree to; the 1999 Act provides a flexible exception. Against: unjust where a contract was made to benefit a third party (Tweddle; Beswick); many exceptions make the law complex; the 1999 Act is often excluded in commercial contracts. Conclusion: Privity remains a sensible starting point, now largely softened by the 1999 Act.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge and understanding [3]: accurate explanation of the law with supporting authority, e.g. Tweddle v Atkinson (1861); Dunlop v Selfridge (1915); Beswick v Beswick (1967); Jackson v Horizon Holidays (1975); Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999. AO3 Analysis and evaluation [5]: arguments supporting the view, e.g. protects parties' freedom of contract; prevents people being bound by contracts they did not agree to; the 1999 Act provides a flexible exception; arguments against / problems, e.g. unjust where a contract was made to benefit a third party (Tweddle; Beswick); many exceptions make the law complex; the 1999 Act is often excluded in commercial contracts. items.stem: Leila bought a hair salon in Mexico City from Ravi. Before the sale Ravi said that the business made a profit of $50 000 a year. In fact it had made a loss for two years. Leila relied on the statement. Leila has just found out the truth after two weeks. Advise Leila on whether there has been an actionable misrepresentation and what remedies are available. Explain the relevant law, apply it to the facts and evaluate the strength of any arguments available.
items.answer: Law: a misrepresentation is a false statement of fact which induces the contract; opinions are not usually statements of fact (Bisset v Wilkinson) unless made by an expert (Esso v Mardon); types: fraudulent (Derry v Peek), negligent under s2(1) MA 1967 (Howard Marine), innocent; rescission may be barred by affirmation or lapse of time (Long v Lloyd; Leaf v International Galleries); damages under s2(1) on the fraud measure (Royscot). Application: Ravi's statement was a false statement of fact; Leila relied on it, so inducement is satisfied (Redgrave v Hurd); Leila has just found out the truth after two weeks, which affects whether rescission is still available. Conclusion: If the statement was a false statement of fact, Leila can probably claim damages under s2(1) MA 1967; rescission depends on whether it is barred by delay or affirmation.

items.stem: Nadia lives in a quiet residential street of Santiago. Arjun held a one-off fireworks display that set fire to Nadia's shed. Nadia complains of damage to property. Advise Nadia whether Arjun has committed a private nuisance and what remedies are available. Explain and apply the relevant law, using decided cases to support your advice.
items.answer: Law: private nuisance is an unreasonable interference with the use or enjoyment of land; the claimant needs a proprietary interest (Hunter v Canary Wharf); factors: locality (Sturges v Bridgman), duration (Crown River Cruises), sensitivity (Robinson v Kilvert), malice (Christie v Davey); coming to the nuisance is no defence (Coventry v Lawrence); remedies: injunction, possibly limited (Kennaway v Thompson), or damages in lieu. Application: Nadia must have a proprietary interest to sue; the area is a quiet residential area where such interference is less acceptable; Arjun's activity is short but caused physical damage (Crown River Cruises). Conclusion: Arjun's conduct is likely to be a nuisance if, weighing these factors, it is unreasonable; Nadia may seek an injunction or damages.

items.stem: Leila agreed to sell Mei a rare vintage car for $40 000. Before completion, Leila received a higher offer and refused to go ahead. Mei waited two years before taking any action. Advise Mei whether a court is likely to order specific performance. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: specific performance is discretionary and granted only where damages are inadequate; land and unique goods are typical examples (Falcke v Gray); it is refused for personal services or where constant supervision is needed (Co-op v Argyll); equitable maxims apply: clean hands; delay defeats equity. Application: the contract was for a rare vintage car: unique goods, so specific performance may be ordered (Falcke v Gray); Mei waited two years before taking any action, which is relevant because delay defeats equity. Conclusion: Unique goods, so specific performance may be ordered (Falcke v Gray), subject to Mei acting promptly.

items.answer: Law: damages aim to put the claimant in the position as if the tort had not occurred; special damages: past lost earnings and expenses; general damages: pain, suffering and loss of amenity (H West v Shephard; Heil v Rankin) and future loss of earnings and care; lump sum or periodical payments (Damages Act 1996); provisional damages where deterioration is possible. Application: Ethan can no longer work and needs daily care; past losses are special damages; pain, suffering and loss of amenity and future losses are general damages; periodical payments may suit long-term care needs. Conclusion: Ethan can claim special damages for past losses and general damages for non-pecuniary and future losses.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain three situations in which a contract may be frustrated. (b) Explain the effect of the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943.
items.answer: (a) Destruction of the subject matter (Taylor v Caldwell); non-occurrence of the event that is the purpose of the contract (Krell v Henry); personal incapacity (Condor v Baron Knights); supervening illegality; government interference; long delay (Jackson v Union Marine). items.stem: On 1 March Noah wrote to Kwame offering to sell a printing machine for $60 000. Kwame received the letter on 3 March and posted a letter of acceptance on the same day. On 4 March Noah emailed Kwame to withdraw the offer. Kwame's letter arrived on 5 March. Advise Kwame whether there is a binding contract. Consider all the relevant issues and reach a justified conclusion.
items.answer: Law: acceptance by post takes effect on posting (Adams v Lindsell); this applies even if the letter is lost (Household Fire v Grant); revocation is effective only when received (Byrne v Van Tienhoven); the offeror may exclude the postal rule (Holwell v Hughes). Application: Kwame posted acceptance on 3 March, so the contract was formed then; Noah's revocation on 4 March came too late; the fact that the letter arrived on 5 March does not matter. Conclusion: A contract was formed on 3 March when Kwame posted the acceptance, so Noah is bound.

AO2 Application [6]: applies the rules to the facts, e.g. Kwame posted acceptance on 3 March, so the contract was formed then; Noah's revocation on 4 March came too late; the fact that the letter arrived on 5 March does not matter. items.stem: Isla took a wedding dress to Leila's tailoring shop in Kathmandu for alteration. Isla signed a form that said in small print: "The company accepts no liability for any damage however caused." The a wedding dress was ruined because of the negligence of Leila's staff. Advise Isla whether Leila can rely on the clause. Explain and apply the relevant law, using decided cases to support your advice.
items.answer: Law: incorporation: a signed document binds (L'Estrange v Graucob) unless its effect was misrepresented (Curtis v Chemical Cleaning); construction: ambiguity is read contra proferentem (Houghton v Trafalgar); CRA 2015: s57 prevents exclusion or restriction of liability for the s49 duty of reasonable care and skill; s62 unfair terms are not binding; s65 death/personal injury cannot be excluded. Application: Isla signed the form, so the clause is incorporated; the clause covers negligence; as a consumer contract for a service, s57 CRA 2015 means Leila cannot exclude or limit liability for failing to use reasonable care and skill. Conclusion: Leila cannot rely on the clause; Isla can claim compensation for the a wedding dress.

items.stem: Samuel negligently drove into a crowd at a festival in Bogotá. Daniel watched the event live on television at home, knowing Daniel's brother was at the festival and later developed post-traumatic stress disorder. Advise Daniel whether Daniel can claim against Samuel for psychiatric injury. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: a recognised psychiatric illness is required; primary victims in the zone of danger recover if physical injury was foreseeable (Page v Smith); secondary victims must satisfy Alcock: close tie, proximity in time and space or immediate aftermath (McLoughlin), own unaided senses; rescuers must be in danger (White v CC South Yorkshire; Chadwick). Application: PTSD is a recognised psychiatric illness; Daniel watched the event live on television at home, knowing Daniel's brother was at the festival; so Daniel is a secondary victim who fails Alcock because there was no perception with own unaided senses and the tie must be proved. Conclusion: Daniel is a secondary victim who fails Alcock because there was no perception with own unaided senses and the tie must be proved.

items.stem: Grace accepted a lift from Felix after a party in Nairobi, knowing that Felix was very drunk. Grace wore a seat belt. Felix crashed and Grace was injured. Advise Felix on the defences available against Grace's claim. Consider all the relevant issues and reach a justified conclusion.
items.answer: Law: volenti requires full knowledge and free acceptance of the risk (Smith v Baker; Morris v Murray), but s149 Road Traffic Act 1988 excludes it for passengers; contributory negligence reduces damages under the 1945 Act; accepting a lift from a drunk driver (Owens v Brimmell) and not wearing a seat belt (Froom v Butcher); illegality may apply to joint criminal enterprises (Pitts v Hunt). Application: volenti cannot apply because of s149 Road Traffic Act 1988; Grace knew Felix was very drunk, so damages may be reduced (Owens v Brimmell); seat belt: no seat belt reduction. Conclusion: Felix cannot rely on volenti, but Grace's damages will be reduced for contributory negligence, including no seat belt reduction.

items.stem: Elena chartered a cargo plane from Aisha for one year to carry goods from Riyadh. The contract stated the cargo plane would be "fit for the purpose". Application: "fit for the purpose" can be broken in trivial or serious ways, so it is innominate; the cargo plane was out of service for three weeks; so Elena was not deprived of substantially the whole benefit, so damages only (Hong Kong Fir). items.stem: Evaluate the doctrine of frustration. Support your answer with relevant authority.
items.answer: For: relieves parties from obligations made impossible by events beyond their control; narrow limits preserve the sanctity of contract (Davis Contractors); 1943 Act provides flexible financial adjustment. Conclusion: The doctrine is a sensible narrow safety valve, with the 1943 Act softening the consequences.

items.answer: (a) s1(3): duty arises if occupier is aware of the danger, knows or believes trespassers may be in the vicinity and the risk is one against which protection is reasonably expected; s1(4): reasonable care to see the trespasser is not injured; s1(5) warnings; s1(6) willing acceptance of risk (Ratcliff); obvious risks from own activity (Tomlinson; Keown); only personal injury is covered (s1(8)). items.stem: Sofia Ltd agreed to repair a bakery oven for Mei Ltd, a printing firm in Manila, within three days. The repair took two weeks longer than agreed. items.stem: Priya agreed to buy a cargo of coffee on board a ship from Ethan for $40 000. Unknown to both of them, it had been destroyed by fire the day before. Advise Priya whether the contract is valid. Your answer should explain the relevant law, refer to decided cases and reach a reasoned conclusion.
items.answer: Law: common mistake as to the existence of the subject matter makes the contract void (Couturier v Hastie); a mistake as to quality does not, unless the subject matter is essentially different (Bell v Lever Bros; Great Peace Shipping). Application: both parties shared the mistake; the mistake was that it had been destroyed by fire the day before, which is res extincta, so the contract is void (Couturier v Hastie). Conclusion: The position is res extincta, so the contract is void (Couturier v Hastie).

items.stem: Omar, a builder aged 41, was seriously injured in an accident caused by Priya's negligence. Omar will need several operations over the next ten years. Explain the types of damages that Omar could claim. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: damages aim to put the claimant in the position as if the tort had not occurred; special damages: past lost earnings and expenses; general damages: pain, suffering and loss of amenity (H West v Shephard; Heil v Rankin) and future loss of earnings and care; lump sum or periodical payments (Damages Act 1996); provisional damages where deterioration is possible. Application: Omar will need several operations over the next ten years; past losses are special damages; pain, suffering and loss of amenity and future losses are general damages; periodical payments may suit long-term care needs. Conclusion: Omar can claim special damages for past losses and general damages for non-pecuniary and future losses.

items.stem: Jonas offered to sell Hana a house for $12 000, promising to keep the offer open until Friday. On Thursday Hana heard from Felix, a reliable mutual friend, that Jonas had sold the house to someone else. On Friday morning Hana sent an acceptance. (a) Identify the main legal issue raised by these facts. (b) Advise Hana whether there is a contract.
items.answer: (a) Revocation of an offer and communication by a third party. (b) Law: an offer can be revoked at any time before acceptance, even if promised to stay open, unless consideration is given (Routledge v Grant); revocation must be communicated (Byrne v Van Tienhoven); communication can be through a reliable third party (Dickinson v Dodds). Application: Hana gave no consideration for the promise to keep the offer open; Hana learned of the sale from Felix, a reliable source, before accepting; so the offer was revoked before acceptance. Conclusion: There is no contract because the offer was effectively revoked before Hana accepted.
